⁋ The board adopted the grandfathering resolution on a 5-4 vote, with Briskman, TeKrony, Vice Chair Mike Turner and Supervisor Sylvia Glass opposed. That same night, supervisors voted 7-2 to change the county’s comprehensive plan and zoning ordinance. ⁋ Those changes made data centers a conditional use in areas where they had previously been considered a core or complementary use, requiring future projects to meet certain conditions before they could be built.
The grandfathering resolution, however, allowed certain pending site plans and amendments
continue through the county’s by-right administrative review process without obtaining the Special Exception required for new data center proposals.

It is time to bring these applications into the public process and give residents a meaningful opportunity to be heard.” ⁋ The county identified more than 20 administrative data center applications as eligible to continue through the by-right approval process under the grandfathering resolution. ⁋ “I am proud to join Supervisor Briskman in her efforts to limit the administrative approval of data center applications,” TeKrony said in a statement. “Loudoun’s electric grid and community are at a breaking point. Residents have had enough of data center sprawl, which is causing unsightly power lines and substations to be built all over the county, near homes and schools and encroaching into our transition and rural policy areas.” ⁋ According to Briskman and TeKrony’s offices, Loudoun County has more than 250 data centers totaling roughly 53 million square feet of development and generating more than $1 billion in annual local tax revenue. The supervisors said continued data center growth has increased demand for electrical infrastructure while contributing to concerns about utility costs, noise, air quality and natural resources, as well as crowding out attainable housing and other forms of economic development. ⁋ Aman Ardalan, Briskman’s senior legislative aid, said the biggest change since March 2025 has been “the intensity of public concern around data center development.” ⁋

⁋ In July, the board voted 6-1 to direct staff to develop a potential moratorium for consideration Sept. 15. County Attorney Leo Rogers has questioned whether Virginia law gives the county authority to impose such a pause and is expected to return with a legal analysis. ⁋ The county is continuing to work on the second phase of its Data Center Standards and Locations initiative, with new regulations expected to be considered by the board in early 2027. The second phase will consider data center standards on setbacks, power usage, height, noise levels, emissions controls and emission standards. ⁋
other localities are contemplating or enacting restrictions

The Frederick County Board of Supervisors has directed staff to draft an ordinance that would remove data centers as an allowed use in all zoning districts. On Tuesday, Chesapeake eliminated by-right development for data centers, while Virginia Beach imposed a yearlong moratorium.
